task: Phase E Track B, B1 (validate carefully), angles: (1) covert/timing side channels and timing-based tamper detection; (2) fraud-detection velocity checks and transaction-timing anomalies. Claim under test is N1, the conditional duration model. Sub-claim (a): duration-vs-expected-workload residuals as a fabrication signal in agent logs. Sub-claim (b): corr(residual, output_size) as the discriminator between work-bound and generation-bound latency.
scope_note: Literature and public documentation only. No corpus data was read or measured. Nothing swarm-related was read. No transcripts were generated. No paid API calls. Sources were opened with WebFetch, the alphaXiv PDF reader (answer_pdf_queries / get_paper_content), or local text extraction of a PDF that WebFetch saved. A source is marked opened=true only if its text, or the named page, was actually retrieved. Quoted passages are kept short. Fields whose names begin with VERDICT_REASONING or INTERPRETATION hold judgement. Every other field is copied from a source.
bottom_line: Neither sub-claim is TAKEN in the agent-log setting by anything found in these two angles. Sub-claim (a) is PARTIAL. Sub-claim (b) is NOVEL, but only within the angles searched here.

(a) The technique is old. It is not new. Mature non-agent systems already flag fraud or tampering by comparing observed duration against a workload-conditioned expectation, often with a within-unit baseline: timing-based attestation (Pioneer 2005; Kovah et al., IEEE S&P 2012, which builds per-host control limits from about 200 repeats of the identical workload), cloud CPU-cheating detection (Zheng/Li/Tan/Wu 2013, actual vs theoretical time of a predefined task), test security (van der Linden's lognormal response-time model, log T = item time-intensity - person speed + e, and Sinharay 2020's within-examinee speed contrast for item preknowledge, implemented in CRAN package 'aberrance'), time-deterministic replay for covert timing channels (Chen et al., OSDI 2014), and the 'impossible day' audit of healthcare billing (summed CPT typical times vs available time). The only thing not found is the application to agent tool-call logs. Frame N1 as a transfer of these methods and cite them as ancestors.

(a), agent-adjacent: the LLM-honeypot literature is the closest neighbour, because those systems fabricate shell or HTTP output with an LLM. It already treats latency as a giveaway. The SoK (arXiv 2510.25939) says timing 'remains a critical and unresolved challenge'. In Honeyval (arXiv 2605.29963), hacking agents 'repeatedly cite response latency and timeouts as evidence'. ShellGames (arXiv 2606.17986) precomputes responses to hide latency. All of them use raw, unconditioned latency, and they use it live, from the attacker's side. None models a workload-conditioned residual from recorded logs.

(b) Only the physical premise is TAKEN. Zhang/Saileshwar/Lie (arXiv 2412.15431) show that LLM generation time is linear in output tokens: Pearson >= 0.987 for local models, but only 0.370 for GPT-4o over the network. They use this as a side channel to infer output length, not to tell generated from executed content. Authorship verification inverts the roles: human typing time scales with text length, and pasted LLM text does not. That literature uses keystroke-interval features, not corr(residual, size). It also explicitly drops characters-per-minute as forgeable (arXiv 2507.22956). No source found uses corr(residual, output_size) to separate work-bound from generation-bound latency.

Material limits for DESIGN.md, from these sources: (1) The strongest timing-attestation schemes let the verifier choose the workload, so that forgery costs time. N1 cannot choose it. Zheng et al. name the matching attack: predict the expected time, then report completion after it. They need a time-lock puzzle to defeat it. A timing-aware forger who pads to the expected duration passes both (a) and (b). (2) Leiner 2019 found that completion time catches careless responses but 'do[es] not allow for detecting intended faking'. Xu & Malkin (SOUPS 2026) found that raw completion time did not separate LLM-using survey takers (median 606.5 s vs 372.0 s, p = .118). Raw duration is not the signal. Conditioning is required. (3) For remote-API generation, the time-vs-length correlation drops sharply (0.370 for GPT-4o), so (b) should be weaker for hosted models than for local ones.

items.claim: Sub-claim (a): duration-vs-expected-workload residuals as a fabrication signal in agent logs (N1).
items.closest_work: Sinharay 2020, 'Detection of Item Preknowledge Using Response Times' (Applied Psychological Measurement), built on van der Linden's lognormal response-time model (JEBS 2006; Psychometrika 2003, 2008). Kovah et al. 2012, 'New Results for Timing-Based Attestation' (IEEE S&P). Zheng/Li/Tan/Wu 2013, 'User-based CPU Verification Scheme for Public Cloud Computing'.
items.what_it_does: Sinharay and van der Linden flag fraudulent test responses from passively logged response times. Log time is modelled as item time-intensity (expected workload) minus person speed, and each examinee's speed on compromised items is compared with the same examinee's speed on other items. Kovah et al. detect code tampering because forgery adds time to a fixed self-checksum, judged against per-host control limits (mean +/- 3 SD from about 200 repeated runs). Zheng et al. flag cloud CPU cheating when the actual time of a predefined task exceeds its theoretical time plus a margin.
items.what_it_does_not: None of them looks at agent tool calls or fabricated tool results. The attestation and cloud schemes need a verifier-chosen workload, plus a correctness check on the returned value, so that faking it costs time. N1 has neither. The psychometric model detects anomalous speed-up from preknowledge. It does not test whether a recorded result was generated rather than executed. In the agent-adjacent LLM-honeypot work, latency is a recognised giveaway of LLM-fabricated output, but only raw latency, judged live. There is no workload-conditioned residual and no log analysis.
items.deciding_citation: Sinharay 2020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7433384): 'The statistic quantifies the difference in speed between the compromised items and the non-compromised items of the examinees.' Kovah et al. 2012 (https://www.mitre.org/sites/default/files/pdf/11_4921.pdf): 'We generate a baseline a system by taking about 200 measurements, and then generate upper and lower control limits (average +/- 3 standard deviation)'. Agent-adjacent: Bridges et al. SoK (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25939): 'timing remains a critical and unresolved challenge' for LLM-based honeypots.

items.claim: Sub-claim (b): corr(residual, output_size) as the discriminator between work-bound latency (real execution) and generation-bound latency (LLM-authored result).
items.closest_work: Zhang, Saileshwar, Lie, 'Time Will Tell: Timing Side Channels via Output Token Count in Large Language Models' (arXiv 2412.15431). Inverse-role analogue: keystroke-based detection of LLM-assisted writing (Roh/Kumar/Ngo, IJCB 2025, arXiv 2507.22956; Gianvecchio et al., USENIX Security 2008, for chat bots).
items.what_it_does: Time Will Tell measures Pearson(generation time, generated tokens): at least 0.987 for local models and 0.370 for GPT-4o through the API. It uses the relationship to recover output token count as a side channel. Keystroke work separates human-typed text from transcribed or pasted LLM text using inter-key timing features. Gianvecchio 2008 uses inter-message delay and message size, as separate entropy features, to tell bots from humans.
items.what_it_does_not: None of them computes the correlation between a workload-conditioned duration residual and output size. None uses such a correlation to decide whether a result was produced by execution or by generation. Time Will Tell never discriminates between process types. The keystroke papers do not correlate per-event duration with produced length. Roh et al. explicitly exclude characters-per-minute metrics as forgeable. Gianvecchio 2008 treats delay and size separately, and notes that bots can be configured so that responses of different lengths take different time to 'type'. That is an evasion, not a detector. The honeypot papers (Honeyval Table 2) report median latency and mean tokens per backend, but never relate per-response latency to response size.
items.deciding_citation: Zhang/Saileshwar/Lie, arXiv 2412.15431 (opened via alphaXiv full text): 'For models running on a local machine, the Pearson coefficient is at least 0.987'. This is the physical premise only. No source found uses the correlation as a provenance discriminator. Verdict bounded to the two assigned angles plus the adjacent areas touched here.

items.claim: N1 design choice: baseline duration from within-unit repeats of the same workload (same command in the same session), so that machine, load and cache state are held constant.
items.closest_work: Kovah et al. 2012 (per-host baseline from repeated identical self-checksum runs). Sinharay 2020 (within-examinee baseline from the same examinee's non-compromised items).
items.what_it_does: Kovah builds per-host control limits from about 200 repeats of the same computation. The paper also finds that TPM tick counts differ per host, so 'each host must be baselined independently'. Sinharay compares each examinee's speed on compromised items with the same examinee's other items.
items.what_it_does_not: Neither uses agent sessions or shell commands. Kovah's repeats are verifier-scheduled, not opportunistic repeats found in a log.
items.deciding_citation: Kovah et al. 2012, conclusion: 'no single expected baseline can be set for different hosts; each host must be baselined independently' (TPM tickstamp result).

items.claim: Context (the basis of the existing latency-floor test): raw latency gives away LLM-fabricated tool or command output.
items.closest_work: LLM-honeypot literature: Bridges et al. SoK (arXiv 2510.25939); Vero et al. Honeyval (arXiv 2605.29963); Salviati et al. ShellGames (arXiv 2606.17986).
items.what_it_does: These honeypots fabricate shell or HTTP responses with an LLM. The SoK lists 'response timing anomalies' as a detection vector, and says an LLM 'Cannot reproduce temporal fidelity or real-time dynamics'. In Honeyval, hacking agents cite latency as evidence of a honeypot, against median backend latencies of 3.3 to 13.7 s. ShellGames speculatively precomputes responses, cutting mean response time from 1.09 s to 0.71 s.
items.what_it_does_not: There is no workload conditioning and no residual model. The judgement is live and adversary-side, not a post-hoc check of a harness log. Honeyval reports 'no clear correlation' between latency and detection rate.
items.deciding_citation: Honeyval, arXiv 2605.29963 section 5.2: hacking agents 'repeatedly cite response latency and timeouts as evidence when classifying the LLM-powered apps as honeypots'.

items.claim: Physical premise of (b): LLM generation latency is linear in output length.
items.what_it_does: States that execution time scales linearly with the number of output tokens because time per output token is roughly constant. Measures Pearson 1.000 (Tower), 0.990 (M2M100), 0.989 (MBart50), 0.987 (Gemma2) locally, and 0.370 for GPT-4o through the API.
items.what_it_does_not: Says nothing about tool calls, fabrication, or the difference between work-bound and generation-bound latency.
items.deciding_citation: arXiv 2412.15431 Table 3, 'Pearson correlation coefficient between token count and generation time': Tower 1.000, M2M100 0.990, MBart50 0.989, Gemma2 0.987, GPT-4o 0.370.

verdict_reasoning.VERDICT_REASONING_a: PARTIAL, not TAKEN and not NOVEL. Several fielded or peer-reviewed systems already flag fraud or tamper from observed duration minus a workload-conditioned expectation, with within-unit baselines: timing attestation, cloud CPU verification, psychometric response-time residuals, time-deterministic replay, and healthcare 'impossible day' audits. That makes the method TAKEN in general. Searched in these angles, nothing applies it to agent tool-call records, where the timestamps are stamped by an honest harness and the result may be fabricated. The LLM-honeypot work recognises latency as a sign of LLM-fabricated tool output, but uses raw latency. The domain application is the only defensible novelty. A reviewer's first objection is likely to be 'this is van der Linden's response-time residual for tool calls' or 'this is timing attestation without the challenge'. Pre-empt it the way CLAUDE_context_swarms.md section 8 pre-empts the Elle objection.
verdict_reasoning.VERDICT_REASONING_b: NOVEL, within the angles searched, at moderate confidence. Three components exist separately: the physics (generation time is linear in output tokens, arXiv 2412.15431); the idea that 'time scales with produced length' is evidence of a sequential producer, in human-authorship verification (inverse roles, different statistic); and the honeypot observation that LLM-fabricated output is slow. No source combines them into the specific test: does the residual left after workload conditioning grow with output size? If it does, the latency is generation-bound and the result was likely authored. If not, the latency is work-bound. The verdict is bounded. Other Phase E agents own the LLM-latency-modelling, machine-generated-text-detection, APM/log-anomaly, CI-runtime and agent-harness angles. Any of those could still contain this statistic.
verdict_reasoning.VERDICT_REASONING_not_taken_either: Neither (a) nor (b) is TAKEN in the agent-log setting by anything found in these angles. (a) is TAKEN as a generic technique outside agents. (b)'s premise is TAKEN, but the discriminator is not.
verdict_reasoning.VERDICT_REASONING_evasion: Both sub-claims fail against a timing-aware forger who controls the tool return and pads the delay to the expected duration. With the residual near zero, (a) passes, and corr(residual, size) becomes uninformative. Zheng et al. 2013 name this attack ('the cloud can predict the execution time ... and then report completion'). They defeat it only by binding timing to a verifiable output (a time-lock puzzle). Agent logs have no such binding. Timing forgery is demonstrated in neighbouring fields: chat bots configured with a 'fixed typing rate' (Gianvecchio 2008), keystroke timing-forgery attacks (arXiv 2601.17280), and survey agents that simulate reading time (Westwood 2025, via secondary source only). N1 is therefore a check against naive inline fabrication, not against adversarial forgery. This matches CLAUDE_context_swarms.md section 8 item 4: necessary, not sufficient.

INTERPRETATION_design_implications: Use the psychometric form directly: log d_ij = beta_cmd(j) - tau_session(i) + e, with sigma per command. It gives a residual with a known null distribution. Sinharay's statistic is standard normal under the null. That lets thresholds be pre-registered (PREREG_E) instead of tuned. Cite van der Linden 2006 and Sinharay 2020 as the model.

Report a raw-duration null alongside N1. Xu & Malkin (SOUPS 2026) and Leiner 2019 both show that unconditioned completion time misses deliberate or LLM-assisted faking. If N1's value comes only from conditioning, show that directly: compare raw duration with the residual on the same calls.

Expect (b) to be weaker for API-hosted generators than for local ones. Time-vs-tokens Pearson was 0.370 for GPT-4o over the network, against at least 0.987 locally (arXiv 2412.15431). Corpora where the fabricating model is a hosted API will dilute the correlation.

Tool Receipts (arXiv 2603.10060) already records duration_ms in every receipt, but leaves it out of the HMAC and never checks it. Instrumented systems therefore already capture the field N1 needs and ignore it. That makes N1 a candidate add-on check for receipt-based systems as well as for uninstrumented logs.

sources.title: Pioneer: Verifying Code Integrity and Enforcing Untampered Code Execution on Legacy Systems (Seshadri, Luk, Shi, Perrig, van Doorn, Khosla), ACM SOSP 2005
sources.saw: Redirected to https://www.cs.umd.edu/~elaine/docs/pioneer.pdf, which returned HTTP 403. https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~arvinds/pubs/pioneer.pdf returned 404. Content is taken from the patent of the same work (S02).

sources.title: US9177153B1, 'Verifying integrity and guaranteeing execution of code on untrusted computer platform' (Perrig, Khosla, Seshadri, Luk, van Doorn; CMU and IBM; priority 2005-10-07)
sources.saw: 'checksum code has to be constructed such that adversarial tampering results in either a wrong checksum or a noticeable time delay'. Also: 'the dispatcher has to know ahead of time what the correct checksum computation time should be'. The baseline comes from a trusted same-CPU platform, a simulator, or published times.

sources.title: New Results for Timing-Based Attestation (Kovah, Kallenberg, Weathers, Herzog, Albin, Butterworth; MITRE), IEEE S&P 2012
sources.saw: Opened via the alphaXiv PDF reader (pp. 1, 3, 7-9, 11, 14). Detects attacks with 'an average of just 1.7% time overhead for the attacker' over 10 network links on 31 hosts. 'a forged checksum takes more time to compute than a genuine one'. 'We generate a baseline a system by taking about 200 measurements ... (average +/- 3 standard deviation)'. Across cross-host comparisons, at most 2 consecutive clean points fell out of control. TPM result: 'each host must be baselined independently'.

sources.title: Tiny-CFA (De Oliveira Nunes, Jakkamsetti, Tsudik), arXiv 2011.07400
sources.saw: Returned by the PDF reader when Pioneer was requested. Background statement: security of software-based attestation 'relies on strong assumptions about precise timing and constant communication delays, which are unrealistic in the IoT/CPS ecosystem'. Cited only for that known limitation.

sources.title: User-based CPU Verification Scheme for Public Cloud Computing (Huanyang Zheng, Kangkang Li, Chiu C. Tan, Jie Wu; Temple University; 2013 per PDF metadata)
sources.saw: PDF saved by WebFetch; text extracted locally with pypdf. Abstract: 'we compare the difference of the actual execution time (recorded by the user) and the theoretical execution time, as to determine whether the cloud is cheating'. Cheating is defined as ta > tt + delta. Worked example: 10^10 instructions at 1 GHz is a theoretical 10 s, against an actual 20 s. Names the attack: 'the cloud can predict the execution time of 10^10 CPU instructions, and then report completion after 10s', countered with a time-lock puzzle.

sources.title: Cloud CPU Verification Scheme for Individual End Users (Zheng, Li, Blaisse, Tan), IJ-CLOSER 2013
sources.saw: Abstract only: 'a user-based CPU verification scheme is proposed for the cloud cheating detection problem, where the cloud service provider offers insufficient CPU resources'. Journal version of S05.

sources.title: Detecting Covert Timing Channels with Time-Deterministic Replay (Chen, Moore, Xiao, Haeberlen, Phan, Sherr, Zhou), USENIX OSDI 2014
sources.saw: Abstract page: timing channels work 'by subtly varying the timing of the machine's outputs, and it is this variation that can be detected with TDR'. Timing is reproduced to within 1.85%. The PDF (web.eecs.umich.edu/~chenang/papers/osdi-2014.pdf) could not be fetched by the PDF reader.

sources.title: US10437993B2, 'Methods, systems, and computer readable media for detecting covert timing channels' (Georgetown University and University of Pennsylvania; priority 2014-10-03)
sources.saw: Claim language: 'comparing the timings of the outputs of the play execution to the timings of outputs of the replay execution to determine whether the output of the play execution contains a covert timing channel'. The expected timing comes from replaying the same inputs, i.e. a workload-exact expectation.

sources.title: Detecting Covert Timing Channels: An Entropy-Based Approach (Gianvecchio, Wang), ACM CCS 2007
sources.saw: PDF saved by WebFetch; text extracted locally. 'a change in the entropy of a process provides a critical clue for covert timing channel detection'. The test inputs are inter-packet delay sequences only, with no conditioning on payload or workload. Representative of covert-channel detectors that are unconditioned on workload.

sources.title: Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs (Gu, Li, Kuditipudi, Liang, Hashimoto), ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.07776
sources.saw: Timing side channel that infers whether work was skipped: 'Cache hits tend to have a faster TTFT than cache misses (after accounting for prompt length)'. Prompt length is held fixed, the two time distributions are compared with a one-sided two-sample KS test, and caching was detected in 8 of 17 providers. The audit is controlled and active, not passive log analysis. Detailed prompt-cache prior art belongs to B3.

sources.title: Time Will Tell: Timing Side Channels via Output Token Count in Large Language Models (Tianchen Zhang, Gururaj Saileshwar, David Lie), arXiv 2412.15431
sources.saw: Full text via alphaXiv. The execution time (T) to generate n tokens 'scales linearly with the number of output tokens'. Table 3, Pearson(token count, generation time): Tower 1.000, M2M100 0.990, MBart50 0.989, Gemma2 0.987, GPT-4o 0.370. Used to leak output length, not to detect fabrication.

sources.title: SoK: Honeypots & LLMs, More Than the Sum of Their Parts? (Bridges, Mitchell, Munoz, Henriksson), arXiv 2510.25939v4
sources.saw: 'Moving to LLM-based honeypots, timing remains a critical and unresolved challenge'. Table 1, LLM fail: 'Cannot reproduce temporal fidelity or real-time dynamics'. Reports that OHRA found latency 'unrealistically slow at times and unusually fast at others'. Earlier honeypot fingerprinting used ICMP/TCP timing statistics. Nothing is conditioned on workload.

sources.title: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots (Vero et al.; ETH Zurich, Google, Google DeepMind), arXiv 2605.29963
sources.saw: Table 2 gives median latency 3.3 s (Gemini 3 Flash) to 13.7 s (Claude Haiku 4.5) and tokens per response 87.7 to 523.9. 'we observe no clear correlation between the honeypots' latency or functional fidelity and the detection rates'. Agents 'repeatedly cite response latency and timeouts as evidence'. No per-response latency-vs-size analysis.

sources.title: ShellGames: Speculative LLM-Driven SSH Deception (Salviati, De Gaspari, Conti, Mancini), arXiv 2606.17986
sources.saw: 'their computational overhead can introduce latency that may alert the adversary'. The Speculative Execution Engine plus Memory Manager cuts mean response time from 1.09 +/- 1.27 s to 0.71 +/- 1.05 s (34.84%). Latency hiding is a design goal. There is no detector.

sources.title: LLM Agent Honeypot: Monitoring AI Hacking Agents in the Wild (Reworr, Volkov; Palisade Research), arXiv 2410.13919v2
sources.saw: Uses timing analysis to separate LLM agents from humans with an absolute threshold. Internal GPT-4o agents had mean 1.20 s and median 1.06 s (N = 173). In-the-wild bots had mean 0.67 s (N = 13,638). 'humans cannot respond as quickly as LLMs'. Not conditioned on output length, and the roles are reversed: the LLM is the client, not the tool.

sources.title: Tool Receipts, Not Zero-Knowledge Proofs: Practical Hallucination Detection for AI Agents (Basu), arXiv 2603.10060
sources.saw: Internal-embodiment check. The receipt struct includes 'duration_ms : 150' and 'timestamp_ms'. The HMAC covers id|tool_name|input_hash|output_hash|timestamp_ms, so duration is not signed. No verification stage uses duration. The deep-agent 'Temporal consistency' check concerns dates inside the output. Records the N1 input field, but N1 itself is absent.

sources.title: Measurement and Classification of Humans and Bots in Internet Chat (Gianvecchio, Xie, Wu, Wang), USENIX Security 2008
sources.saw: Two metrics, inter-message delay and message size, treated as separate entropy and machine-learning features. Responder-bot evasion: 'The bot can be configured with a fixed typing rate, so that responses with different lengths take different time to type.' The paper does not use the delay-size relationship as a detector.

sources.title: LLM-Assisted Cheating Detection in Korean Language via Keystrokes (Roh, Kumar, Ngo), IEEE IJCB 2025, arXiv 2507.22956
sources.saw: Keystroke timing separates bona fide, paraphrased and transcribed (LLM) writing, n = 69. 'Aggregate fluency metrics (e.g., characters, words, or sentences per minute) were excluded because they are susceptible to manipulation through artificial pacing.'

sources.title: Detecting LLM-Assisted Academic Dishonesty using Keystroke Dynamics (Mehta, Kumar, Singla, Bisht, Singla, Shah), arXiv 2511.12468
sources.saw: Features are key-hold and key-interval times, pauses and editing patterns. Per the WebFetch reading, no response-length-vs-time analysis appears.

sources.title: On the Insecurity of Keystroke-Based AI Authorship Detection: Timing-Forgery Attacks Against Motor-Signal Verification (Condrey), arXiv 2601.17280
sources.saw: Abstract: such defenses are insecure against 'timing-forgery attacks, in which automated agents sample inter-keystroke intervals from empirical human distributions'. Abstract page only.

sources.title: Prolific researcher help: 'How do I prevent AI-generated responses in my study?'
sources.saw: Production system, internal-embodiment check. Advises against adding 'your own typing-speed or screen-focus checks. These signals are already part of what Prolific's bot and LLM checks analyse.' States 'LLM checks work with 98.7% precision' (vendor claim). The statistic is not disclosed, so it is unknown whether time is conditioned on response length.

sources.title: A Penny for Your Prompts: Experiments Detecting and Mitigating LLM Usage by Survey Respondents (Zane Xu, Nathan Malkin), SOUPS 2026, arXiv 2607.00403
sources.saw: N = 250 (199 in the main analyses). Raw completion time did not flag LLM users: suspected LLM users had median 606.5 s vs 372.0 s, U = 3061.0, p = .118. Speeder screening 'is not sufficient in the age of AI'. Copy-paste events were the reliable signal. No time-per-length test.

sources.title: Too Fast, too Straight, too Weird: Non-Reactive Indicators for Meaningless Data in Internet Surveys (Leiner), Survey Research Methods 13(3):229-248, 2019, doi 10.18148/srm/2019.v13i3.7403
sources.saw: Abstract: careless responses are 'most reliably identified by questionnaire completion time, but the tested indicators do not allow for detecting intended faking'. Proposes a completion speed index. The 1KA help page (https://www.oneclicksurvey.com/d/help/user-guide/dashboard/speed-index, opened) implements a per-page speed index against the per-page median.

sources.title: A Lognormal Model for Response Times on Test Items (van der Linden), JEBS 31(2):181-204, 2006, doi 10.3102/10769986031002181
sources.saw: Abstract: the model has 'a parameter for the speed of each person as well as parameters for the time intensity and discriminating power of each item'.

sources.title: Using Response Times to Detect Aberrant Responses in Computerized Adaptive Testing (van der Linden, van Krimpen-Stoop), Psychometrika 68(2):251-265, 2003, doi 10.1007/BF02294800
sources.saw: Abstract: 'A lognormal model for response times is used to check response times for aberrances in examinee behavior'. Classical and Bayesian posterior-predictive checks.

sources.title: Bayesian Procedures for Identifying Aberrant Response-Time Patterns in Adaptive Testing (van der Linden, Guo), Psychometrika 73(3):365-384, 2008, doi 10.1007/s11336-007-9046-8
sources.saw: Abstract: it is important 'to separate the speed at which the test taker operates from the time the items require'. Includes a power study with simulated cheating. GMAT data.

sources.title: Detection of Item Preknowledge Using Response Times (Sinharay), Applied Psychological Measurement, 2020
sources.saw: 'The statistic quantifies the difference in speed between the compromised items and the non-compromised items of the examinees.' Signed likelihood-ratio and Wald forms, standard normal under the null. The baseline is within-examinee.

sources.title: CRAN package 'aberrance' 0.1.1, detect_pk
sources.saw: Implements the response-time preknowledge statistics 'L_T' (signed likelihood ratio) and 'W_T' (Wald), citing Sinharay 2020. Shows the method is shipped as software, not only published.

sources.title: Bayesian Analysis of Aberrant Response and Response Time Data (Zhang, Zhang, Lu), Frontiers in Psychology 2022
sources.saw: States the model explicitly: 'log(Tij) = lambda_j - tau_i + e_ij', where lambda_j is item time intensity and tau_i is examinee speed. Applied to rapid guessing.

sources.title: Stripe Radar rules: supported attributes
sources.saw: Velocity attributes are counts in fixed windows, e.g. 'authorized_charges_per_card_number_hourly' and 'total_transactions_per_ip_address_hourly'. Elapsed-time attributes include 'seconds_since_customer_was_created' and 'hours_since_card_first_seen'. Nothing conditions time on the size of the work.

sources.title: Microsoft Entra ID Protection: What are risk detections?
sources.saw: Impossible travel: 'activities ... originating from geographically distant locations within a time period shorter than the time it takes to travel from the first location to the second'. A physics-bound floor on elapsed time, given distance as the workload. Atypical travel has a learning period of 14 days or 10 logins.

sources.title: Frier Levitt, 'Physician Billing: Defending the Impossible Day Case' (2017-09-20)
sources.saw: 'Federal prosecutors rely upon an aggregation of the typical times in the AMA's CPT Manual that are associated with different codes to prove fraud under the impossible day theory.' Claimed work, at expected per-item durations, is compared with the time available.

sources.title: Airbridge glossary: Click to install time (CTIT)
sources.saw: Click injection 'produces an abnormally short CTIT, often just seconds'. Click spamming produces 'an abnormally long CTIT distribution'. Per the WebFetch reading, there is no conditioning of CTIT thresholds on app size or download time.

sources.title: Adjust glossary: CTIT
sources.saw: HTTP 429. A search-result summary said larger apps lengthen CTIT. That claim is UNVERIFIED.

sources.title: Temporal Anomaly Detection in Business Processes (Rogge-Solti, Kasneci), BPM 2014, LNCS
sources.saw: Repository page with a partial abstract. Temporal anomalies in activity runtimes are detected with 'a Bayesian model that can be automatically inferred form the Petri net representation of a business process'. The Springer chapter (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-10172-9_15) redirected to a login page and was not opened. The process-mining and APM angle belongs to other B1 agents.

sources.title: The potential existential threat of large language models to online survey research (Westwood), PNAS 122(47):e2518075122, 2025
sources.saw: HTTP 403.
